CALENDAR: Data types · set up Python on your laptop
Exam 2 · Data structures and OOP (9:00 am, pencil)
Discussion: Python vs C vs Java

SECTIONS.title: Data types and expressions
ideas: Python has four everyday types: int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (text in quotes) and bool (True/False). type(x) tells you which one you have.
Arithmetic: + - * as usual, / always gives a float, // is floor division, % is the remainder and ** is a power. Normal precedence rules apply; parentheses win.
A variable is a name bound to a value with =. Assignment is not an equation: x = x + 1 means “make x one bigger”. Comparisons use ==.
input() always returns a string, so convert with int() or float() before doing math. str() goes the other way.
f-strings put values inside text: f"{name} is {age}", with formatting such as {price:.2f}. print() takes many arguments and puts spaces between them.

SECTIONS.title: Modules and turtle graphics
ideas: A module is a file of ready-made code. import math then math.sqrt(2); or from math import sqrt to use sqrt(2) directly; or import random as r to shorten the name.
math has sqrt, floor, ceil, pi, sin, cos; random has randint(a, b) (both ends included), random() (0 up to 1) and choice(list).
The turtle module draws by moving a pen: forward(d), backward(d), left(deg), right(deg), penup()/pendown(), goto(x, y), circle(r), color(...), begin_fill()/end_fill().
The turtle starts at (0, 0) facing east (right); angles turn counter-clockwise for left. The screen’s y axis points up, unlike most graphics systems.

Events make drawings interactive: screen.onkey(func, "Up"), screen.onclick(func), screen.ontimer(func, ms), then screen.listen() and screen.mainloop(). You pass the function name, without parentheses.

SECTIONS.title: Functions
ideas: def name(parameters): defines a function; the indented body runs only when the function is called with name(arguments).
return value hands a result back to the caller and ends the function. A function with no return returns None. Printing is not returning.
Parameters are local: variables created inside a function vanish when it ends. A function can read a global variable but should take what it needs as parameters.
Default values (def greet(name, punct="!")) make arguments optional. Keyword arguments (greet(punct="?", name="Al")) can come in any order.
Design: one job per function, a docstring that says what it does, and small functions that call each other. Test each one alone before wiring them together.

SECTIONS.title: Selection: if, elif, else
ideas: if condition: runs a block when the condition is true; elif tests another condition only if the earlier ones failed; else catches everything else. Only one branch of a chain runs.
Comparisons: == != < <= > >=. Combine with and, or, not; and binds tighter than or, so use parentheses when mixing.
Chained comparisons read like math: 0 <= x < 10.
Every value has a truth value: 0, 0.0, "", [] and None are false; everything else is true.
Nested ifs work, but flat elif chains are easier to read. Put the most specific test first when ranges overlap.

SECTIONS.title: Strings
ideas: A string is a sequence of characters. Index from 0: s[0] is the first character, s[-1] the last, len(s) the length.
Slices copy a piece: s[a:b] is characters a up to but not including b; leave out an end to go to the edge; s[::-1] reverses.
Strings are immutable: methods give back a new string. upper() lower() strip() replace(a, b) split() find(x) count(x) startswith(x) isdigit(). Use ", ".join(list) to glue pieces.
+ joins, * repeats, in tests for a substring, and a for ch in s loop visits each character.
Escape sequences: \n newline, \t tab, \" a quote. ord("A") is 65 and chr(66) is "B".

SECTIONS.title: Iteration: for and while
ideas: for x in something: repeats the body once per item: characters of a string, numbers from range(), later items of a list.
range(n) is 0 to n−1; range(a, b) is a to b−1; range(a, b, step) can count by 2 or backwards with a negative step.
The accumulator pattern: start a total (or count, or string) before the loop and update it inside: total += x.
while condition: repeats as long as the condition is true. Something in the body must move toward making it false, or the loop never ends.
break leaves the loop early; continue skips to the next turn. Nested loops run the inner loop completely for each turn of the outer one.

SECTIONS.title: Recursion
ideas: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. It needs a base case that answers directly and a recursive case that shrinks the input toward the base case.
Classic shapes: factorial(n) = n * factorial(n - 1) with factorial(0) = 1; sum of a list = first item + sum of the rest; countdown; digit sum; powers.
Each call gets its own local variables and waits on the call stack until the deeper call returns. Too deep (no base case) gives RecursionError.
Turtle recursion draws trees, spirals and snowflakes: draw one piece, then call yourself with a shorter length until it is too small.
Anything recursive can be written with a loop; recursion is chosen when the problem is naturally self-similar.

SECTIONS.title: Computer memory: how values are stored
ideas: Memory is a huge row of bytes, each of 8 bits. Everything (numbers, text, code) is stored as patterns of bits; 2<sup>10</sup> = 1024 bytes is a kibibyte, and binary 1011 is 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.
A Python variable is a name that refers to an object somewhere in memory. id(x) shows the address; two names can refer to the same object.
Ints, floats and strings are immutable: y = x; y += 1 makes y refer to a new object and leaves x alone. Lists (soon) are mutable, so two names for the same list see each other’s changes.
Floats are binary fractions with limited precision, which is why 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False. Compare floats with a tolerance or round().
Function calls stack up frames (their local variables); a frame is freed when the call returns. Python frees objects nobody refers to anymore.

SECTIONS.title: Lists
ideas: A list holds items in order: scores = [90, 85, 77]. Index and slice like strings, but lists are mutable: scores[0] = 95 changes it in place.
Growing and shrinking: append(x), insert(i, x), remove(x) (first match), pop() (last item, returned) or pop(i). len, sum, min, max, sorted work on lists.
lst.sort() sorts in place and returns None; sorted(lst) returns a new sorted list and leaves the original alone. Same with reverse() versus lst[::-1].
Two names can share one list (b = a). To copy, use a[:] or list(a). Passing a list to a function lets the function change it.
Lists of lists make tables: grid[row][col]. text.split() turns a string into a list of words; " ".join(lst) goes back.

SECTIONS.title: Files
ideas: with open("data.txt") as f: opens a file and closes it automatically at the end of the block. Modes: "r" read (default), "w" write (erases!), "a" append.
Reading: for line in f: visits each line (with its trailing \n, so strip() it); f.read() gives the whole text; f.readlines() a list of lines.
Writing: f.write(text) writes exactly what you give it, so add \n yourself. Numbers must be converted with str() or an f-string.
CSV-style data: split each line on the delimiter, line.strip().split(","), convert the fields you need, and accumulate totals, counts or a list of records.
A missing file raises FileNotFoundError; check the name and that the file sits next to your program (or give a full path).

SECTIONS.title: Dictionaries
ideas: A dictionary maps keys to values: ages = {"Ana": 19, "Ben": 20}. Look up with ages["Ana"], add or change with ages["Cy"] = 18, remove with del ages["Ben"] or pop.
A missing key raises KeyError; ages.get("Zed", 0) returns a default instead. "Ana" in ages tests keys, not values.
Loop over ages (keys), ages.values() or ages.items() for key–value pairs. sorted(ages) gives the keys in order.
The counting pattern: counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1. Grouping: a dictionary whose values are lists.
Keys must be immutable (strings, numbers, tuples). Values can be anything, including lists and other dictionaries.

SECTIONS.title: Classes and objects: the basics
ideas: A class is a blueprint; an object (instance) is one thing built from it: p = Point(3, 4). Each object has its own attributes (data) and shares the class’s methods (functions).
__init__(self, ...) runs when an object is created and sets its attributes with self.x = x. self is the object the method is working on; Python passes it automatically.
Methods are called with a dot: p.move(1, 2). Inside, self.x reads or changes that object’s state, so calling a method can change the object.
__str__(self) returns the text print(p) shows. Other special methods: __eq__ for ==, __lt__ for sorting.
Objects can be stored in lists and dictionaries and passed to functions. A list of objects plus a loop is the heart of most programs.

SECTIONS.title: More object orientation: inheritance
ideas: Inheritance: class Dog(Animal): makes Dog a kind of Animal. Dog gets every attribute and method of Animal and can add or replace some.
Overriding: define a method with the same name in the subclass to replace it. Call the parent version with super().method(), especially super().__init__(...) to set up inherited attributes.
isinstance(d, Animal) is True for a Dog. Python looks for a method on the object’s class first, then its parents.
Class attributes (defined in the class body) are shared by all objects; instance attributes (self.x) belong to one object. A class attribute is handy for counting objects.
Composition: an object can hold other objects (a Course holds a list of Students). Prefer “has a” (composition) unless something really “is a” (inheritance).

SECTIONS.title: OOP principles
ideas: Abstraction: a class exposes a simple interface (its methods) and hides the messy details. You use acct.deposit(20) without knowing how the balance is stored.
Encapsulation: data and the code that works on it live together; attributes are changed through methods that keep the object valid. A leading underscore (_balance) says “internal”.

Inheritance: shared behavior lives once in a parent class; subclasses specialize. Polymorphism: different classes answer the same method name in their own way, so a loop over mixed objects just calls speak().
Design steps: list the nouns (classes) and verbs (methods) in the problem, decide what each object must remember, then write __init__ and __str__ first.
Python is “duck-typed”: any object with the right methods works, whether or not it inherits from a common parent.

SECTIONS.title: NumPy arrays
ideas: import numpy as np. An array holds many numbers of one type and does math on all of them at once: a * 2, a + b, a ** 2 (element-wise, no loop).
Making arrays: np.array([1, 2, 3]), np.arange(0, 10, 2), np.linspace(0, 1, 5), np.zeros(4), np.ones((2, 3)), np.random.randint(1, 7, size=10).
a.shape, a.size, a.dtype. Index and slice like lists; 2-D arrays use a[row, col], a[:, 0] for a column.
Boolean masks filter: a[a > 5]; (a > 5).sum() counts. Reductions: a.sum(), a.mean(), a.max(), a.argmax(), a.std(), with axis=0 down columns or axis=1 across rows.
Arrays are the fast, memory-light way to hold data; pandas and matplotlib are built on them.

SECTIONS.title: matplotlib
ideas: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt. The usual recipe: prepare x and y data, call a plot function, add labels, then plt.show() (or savefig).
Plot types: plt.plot(x, y) lines, plt.scatter(x, y) points, plt.bar(labels, heights), plt.hist(values, bins=10), plt.pie(sizes, labels=...).
Dress it up: plt.title, plt.xlabel, plt.ylabel, plt.legend() (needs label= on each series), plt.grid(True), colors and markers ("ro--").
Several series: call plot twice before show. Several panels: fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2) then axes[0].plot(...).
A good chart answers one question: pick the type that shows it (trend over time = line, category comparison = bar, distribution = histogram, relationship = scatter).

SECTIONS.title: pandas DataFrames
ideas: import pandas as pd. A DataFrame is a table with named columns; a Series is one column. pd.read_csv("file.csv") loads data; pd.DataFrame({...}) builds one from lists.
First look: df.head() (5 rows), df.shape, df.columns, df.info(), df.describe().
Select: df["col"] a column, df[["a", "b"]] several, df.loc[row_label, "col"] by label, df.iloc[0] by position. Filter with a mask: df[df["score"] > 80].
Compute: df["col"].mean(), .max(), .value_counts(), df.sort_values("col", ascending=False), new columns df["pct"] = df["score"] / 100.
Group: df.groupby("major")["score"].mean() answers “average per group”. df.plot(...) hands the table to matplotlib.

SECTIONS.title: Python vs C vs Java, and the final
ideas: Python is interpreted and dynamically typed: you run source code directly and a variable can hold any type. C and Java are compiled and statically typed: every variable declares a type and mistakes are caught before running.

Speed: compiled C runs many times faster than Python; Java sits between (compiled to bytecode, run by a virtual machine). Python wins on writing speed and libraries, which is why data science lives there.
Memory: C makes you manage memory by hand (malloc/free); Java and Python collect garbage automatically. Python indents blocks; C and Java use braces and semicolons.
Same idea, three spellings: a for loop, a function, a class look alike once you know one language. CSCI 132 continues in a compiled language.
Final exam prep: it is the third equally weighted exam and centers on Unit 4 (NumPy, matplotlib, pandas), but the reading-code skills from Units 1–3 are assumed.
